title: The 2026–27 El Niño

charter.in: The El Niño that formed in the tropical Pacific in June 2026, followed from the first forecasts of its onset (March 2026) through its threshold crossing, agency declarations and growth toward a forecast record-strong peak around the end of 2026. A story belongs when it reports on the event itself (onset odds, declarations, strength readings such as the Niño 3.4 anomaly, peak and duration forecasts) or on impacts and responses our story presents as this El Niño's, with El Niño as the story's subject.
out: the 2023–24 El Niño and its after-effects
research on El Niño in general (coral records of past variability, future-frequency models, conflict links)
global temperature, sea-surface temperature and ocean-heat records
Earth's energy imbalance and WMO state-of-the-climate reports
the northeast Pacific marine heatwave off North America
Indonesia's 2026 fire and haze season (optional only where our story names El Niño as a main driver)
US cuts to ocean observing networks
other drivers of the 2026 food crisis (Strait of Hormuz shipping, Ukraine grain exports, aid cuts)
Panama's drought where our story does not attribute it to El Niño
charter.endEvent: Any one of the forecasting agencies (NOAA, WMO, JMA or the Australian Bureau of Meteorology) declares the El Niño over: ENSO-neutral or La Niña conditions have returned.

figures.name: Chance of El Niño conditions
figures.definition: A forecasting agency's probability (NOAA, WMO, PAGASA, …) that El Niño conditions of any strength will be present in the target season the story names, whether forming or persisting into that season. Dated to the story, since the forecasts' issue dates are not given. Not the chance of a strong or very strong event, and not the chance of a record-hot year.
variants: chance it persists into a later season (in our pull quotes only: 96% for December–February, 97% for the first half of 2027, near-100% through February 2027)
chance of a moderate El Niño only (BMKG, Indonesia): matches false

figures.name: Chance of a very strong El Niño
figures.definition: A forecaster's probability that this event reaches very strong ('super') strength: NOAA's very strong category (a Niño 3.4 anomaly of about 2°C or more) or an equivalent agency category. Not the chance of El Niño of any strength.
variants: 'very strong', ranking among the largest since 1950 (NOAA CPC)
'very strong' from October 2026 to January 2027 (PAGASA, 81%, in a pull quote only)

figures.name: Niño 3.4 sea-surface temperature anomaly
figures.definition: Observed departure of sea-surface temperature from normal in the Niño 3.4 region of the central-eastern equatorial Pacific, the index behind NOAA's ONI (El Niño threshold +0.5°C; very strong about +2°C). Forecast peaks, subsurface readings, local hotspots and other regions do not match.
variants: forecast peak or seasonal anomaly (more than 2°C, about 3°C, 3.7°C, up to 3.8°C, 4.0°C)
local readings 'in places' or 'in parts of the Pacific'
'Pacific temperature anomaly' with the index unstated

notes:
BOUNDARY RULE, applied the same way to every candidate. MUST: the 2026–27 El Niño is the story's subject, either the event itself (onset odds, the threshold crossing, agency declarations, strength readings, peak and duration forecasts) or impacts and responses the story presents as this El Niño's, with El Niño the subject of the title or the opening summary sentence (WFP and UN hunger projections, AfDB costs, Goldman Sachs food prices, Peru's anchovy ban, the Panama Canal caps, UNICEF, Papua New Guinea, California, Southeast Asia, the 451,000 heat-death projection). Impact stories that pass this test are must, not optional: an ongoing-story page about this El Niño would carry them. OPTIONAL: (a) the subject is an impact or response with a life of its own, the story names this El Niño as a main driver, but the cause is shared with land clearing or long-term warming (Indonesia's 2026 fire season, 6 stories; India's monsoon-shortfall plan; Brazil's wildfire budget; Indonesia's peat food estates; rice yields; a disaster-finance commentary); or (b) the story is about something else but carries a real update on the event (a science roundup, an ocean-monitoring op-ed with NOAA's confirmation and 63% odds, a global sea-surface outlook framed on the forming El Niño, a coral-trend feature that opens on this event, the WMO climate-state update titled on El Niño). OUT (near misses): El Niño named only as one factor or a future risk in stories about temperature, sea-surface or ocean-heat records, the energy imbalance, deforestation, heat, wildfires in general or war-driven food crises; research on El Niño in general; the 2023–24 El Niño; the 2025 La Niña. The 'El Niño' title label is not decisive: three labelled stories are near misses (general research) and two are optional. Same-day duplicates (6 Jun WMO, 1 Aug WMO, 6/7 Aug WFP) are all entries; at most one of each set is a turning point.

VALUES. Taken only from title, summary, relevance reasons and antifactors, as the format lists (no entry with a value has research paragraphs). The pull quotes state four more numbers, left out for that reason: NOAA's 96% for December 2026–February 2027 (23 May), PAGASA's 81% chance of 'very strong' and 97% chance of persisting into the first half of 2027 (2 Sep), and WMO's near-100% persistence through February 2027 (9 Oct); an evaluator should not penalize a system that extracts them. Ranges are recorded as their lower bound with approx at_least (80–90% gives 80; BMKG's 50–60% gives 50). Forecast probabilities are dated to the story. The 1 Aug monthly Niño 3.4 values are dated to the month's last day (April 0.5°C on 2026-04-30, June 1.6°C on 2026-06-30). Only three entries state an observed Niño 3.4 anomaly (6 Jun about 1°C, 1 Aug 0.5 then 1.6°C, 22 Sep 3.05°C); forecast peaks and 'in places', 'parts of the Pacific' and subsurface readings are matches false. The 22 Sep 3.05°C is called 'the Pacific temperature anomaly' without naming the index, and its antifactors warn that raw and ONI baselines differ: kept as matching, but uncertain. Not values: Trenberth's 'above 2 degrees Celsius' (21 Jun) defines very strong, and the 9 Oct 'previous 2.6°C record' belongs to an earlier El Niño.
